At a neighborhood market, a shorter line is an attractive promise. The market committee therefore proposes requiring every stall to accept payment through one phone app and to stop taking cash. Digital records would make the day's accounts easier to check, and sellers would spend less time finding change. These are real advantages. They do not, however, settle the question of whether cash should disappear.
Consider the customers who already use the app. For them, the change may seem minor. Yet a shopper whose phone battery runs out would suddenly be unable to pay, despite having money in a pocket. A visitor who does not use that app would face the same barrier. The market would still display the same goods at the same prices, but it would no longer offer the same opportunity to buy them.
The committee also argues that a single method would simplify sellers' work. This is reasonable during an ordinary busy morning. It is less convincing when a connection fails. A reserve payment method could keep some sales moving while the problem is fixed. Cash creates work of its own, including counting and storage, so keeping it is not cost-free. The committee should compare these costs with the cost of turning customers away.
A trial allowing both methods would provide better evidence than a rule based mainly on faster lines. The market could record waiting times and failed purchases, then judge convenience from both sides of the counter. Efficiency deserves attention, but so does the ability to complete a purchase.
q: Which recommendation best represents the writer's position?
choices: Choose one app after comparing several providers.
Test both methods before deciding whether to end cash.
Keep cash for visitors and use the app for local buyers.
Let each stall run its own separate payment trial.

At the checkout display, pick up either of two cereal boxes. Their printed barcodes are identical, although one box has a red sale sticker. Scan the same box at two demonstration counters representing different shops. Each screen shows a different price. Nothing has gone wrong: the demonstration separates what this kind of barcode carries from what the shop's computer knows.
The familiar pattern of dark bars and light spaces represents an identifying number. For ordinary packaged goods like these, the number serves as a key to information stored elsewhere. The scanner reads it, and the shop's system looks up the product's name and price in its records. A price change can therefore be made in those records without printing a new barcode on every box. Other kinds of codes can carry different information, so this demonstration concerns the standard product labels used here.
Next, move to the stock display. Several packages of the same cereal share a product number. Scanning a sale can help a store update how many packages it has left, provided that its stock records are maintained. The printed label does not change as the stock falls. It identifies a product type rather than giving each physical box a separate personal name.
Finally, compare the label with the information on the screen. A successful scan shows that a code can be read. It does not, by itself, prove that every record is correct. If someone enters the wrong price, a clear barcode can lead directly to that wrong information. The pattern is one part of a larger system.
q: What understanding is this display mainly designed to develop?
choices: Product codes work together with stored records.
Product labels store a shop's current selling prices.
Stock systems give every box a personal number.
Changing a price requires a new code on each box.
explain: 各展示都串起條碼與後端紀錄的分工。stored records＝儲存的紀錄；相同商品可共用號碼，並非每盒各有專屬號碼。

Dear Jamie, You asked why our library app puts you on a waiting list for a book that has no paper pages. You thought we might be short of computer storage. The delay is understandable, but adding space would not solve this particular problem. For the title you requested, our library pays for permission to lend a digital copy to one reader at a time. We currently have three such copies. When all three are borrowed, the next reader has to wait.
That limit comes from the lending agreement, rather than from the difficulty of making another file. Other titles may come with different agreements, including access for several readers at once. This is why one book may be available immediately while another has a waiting list. The difference does not necessarily tell you which file is larger or which app feature works better.
You suggested buying more copies of the popular title. We are considering it. However, the same budget also provides less-requested books for readers with different interests. Spending everything on today's longest waiting list could leave fewer choices tomorrow. Our staff considers both waiting times and the range of books available.
Meanwhile, if you finish early, please return your copy through the app rather than simply closing it. The app will then release that copy for the next reader. You may also find another edition or a paper copy in our catalogue. Neither suggestion changes the lending limit, but both can help readers spend less time waiting. Thank you for asking how the service works. Mina, library assistant

To explain how to add storage space to the system
To announce that the library will buy more copies
To explain digital waiting lists and suggest options

A visitor returns to a gallery hoping to see a favorite watercolor and finds a different picture in its place. The missing work has not necessarily been sold or sent abroad. It may be in a dark storage room. For delicate works on paper, spending time out of sight can be part of remaining available to future visitors.
Light allows us to enjoy an image, but it can also change its colors. The damage adds up: a weak light over many hours can harm a sensitive work, just as stronger light can over a shorter period. Putting a faded picture in darkness does not bring back its lost color. Protective glass can filter out certain harmful rays, but the visible light needed for viewing can still cause damage.
At one gallery, staff record both the lighting conditions and the time each drawing spends on display. These records guide later decisions about when it can be shown again. Works are exchanged before visitors can easily notice a change in them. A photograph of an absent picture remains available, clearly identified as a reproduction.
Such a schedule involves a difficult balance. Keeping everything in storage would protect the collection from light but deny people the experience of seeing the actual works. Keeping favorites permanently on the wall would serve today's visitors at the expense of tomorrow's. Friday, after the concert. My task sounded simple when the pianist invited me to turn her pages: stand, turn a sheet, and sit down again. At rehearsal, however, she asked me to follow the music rather than count seconds. She sometimes slowed a phrase and sometimes moved ahead. A turn made at a fixed moment could hide notes she was still reading.
We worked through the printed music together. Several passages were repeated, and one page had to stay open while she played a section again. I marked the route through these passages in pencil. This gave me a way to follow the order without covering the notes. We also agreed that a small nod would tell me when she was ready for the next page.
During the concert, a sudden cough from the audience put me on edge. For a moment, I lost my place. My finger was ready to lift the sheet when I heard the opening notes of the repeated passage. I lowered my hand and waited. The pianist gave the nod much later, after she had completed the return.
Afterward, a friend asked whether I had enjoyed sitting so close to the piano. I had, but not as a listener free to let my thoughts wander. The pencil marks gave me a plan; the sound told me where we actually were. I had spent the evening making tiny decisions whose success depended on their being almost unnoticed.
q: Which title best captures the writer's concert experience?
choices: The Cough That Changed a Pianist's Interpretation
Why Repeated Passages Reduce a Concert's Appeal
The Decisions Behind a Simple Page Turn
A Listener's Guide to Recognizing Musical Phrases
explain: 從排練、失去位置到靠聆聽判斷，重點是翻譜也須決策。page turn＝翻譜；咳嗽影響翻譜者，未改變鋼琴家的詮釋。

Interviewer: Your translations for films are often shorter than the original speech. Why? Translator: A viewer has to read while watching faces and actions. A sentence that sounds natural aloud may take too long to read on screen. I try to preserve the speaker's intention while reducing the amount of text. Shortening is a decision about meaning, not simply a way to squeeze words into limited space.
Interviewer: What about jokes? Translator: In one comedy, a character gives a serious explanation and then adds a word that changes everything. An early translation revealed that word immediately. People reading it could understand the joke before the actor finished speaking. I revised the wording and the timing so the surprise arrived with the final word. A translation can convey the right information and still spoil a scene.
Interviewer: Can you judge your work by reading the translated lines alone? Translator: That helps me notice awkward language, but it is not enough. I watch the scene again with the finished text. Once, I had trimmed a character's repeated refusal to a single polite reply. On its own, the line seemed clear. Beside the actor's angry gestures, it made him seem strangely calm.
Interviewer: What tells you a version is ready? Translator: I ask someone unfamiliar with the film to watch it. I want to know what that person understands about the characters, and whether reading leaves time to see them. My knowledge of the story can hide problems that a new viewer notices at once.
q: What does the interview mainly help readers understand?
choices: How actors help translators simplify their lines.
How viewers can read faster while watching films.
How comedy creates a need for longer translations.
How film translators balance several demands.

Reader: I used a word from a dictionary in a letter asking a company for work. My teacher said it sounded too casual. If the dictionary includes it, why can I not use it? Language adviser: A dictionary tells you more than whether a word exists. It may also tell you where the word belongs. Listing a word is not a promise that it suits every situation.
Look beside the meaning you selected. A label such as informal gives information about the setting in which an expression is normally used. A word can be friendly in a conversation and unsuitable in a formal request. Similarly, an expression marked old-fashioned may help you understand a historical novel without being a good choice for a current advertisement. These labels describe different limits; they are not all warnings that a word is rude.
Examples matter too. A dictionary may give several senses of one word, but a sentence illustrates only a particular use. Compare the sentence around the word in your source with the examples beside that sense. Then try a complete sentence of your own. If you check only a short definition, you may miss the relationship between the word and its neighbors.
For your letter, begin with what you want the company to understand. Choose a possible word, read its labels, and compare its examples with your sentence. A dictionary becomes more useful when you approach it with a situation in mind, rather than treat its pages as a box of words that can be exchanged freely.

Dear Rosa, You asked what Midsummer in Sweden looks like beyond the photographs of flowers. I spent the holiday with Lina's family, then joined a public celebration nearby. Together, the two gatherings gave me a fuller picture than either could have provided alone. I should add that I am describing the people I met, not a set of rules followed by every Swedish family.
In the morning, we helped decorate a tall pole with leaves and flowers. Later, people gathered around it for songs and dances. At the public gathering, someone called out movements so newcomers could follow. Lina's grandfather joined one dance and watched the next. Nobody seemed concerned about turning the afternoon into a polished performance. There was space to take part without displaying any special ability.
Back at the house, relatives made flower crowns while preparing the table. Lina's mother said that their family repeated the same lunch menu because it connected the day with earlier summers. Yet the table also held a dish brought by a cousin's new partner. They were happy to make room for it. The familiar meal and the new food belonged to the same afternoon.
I had tried to plan the visit around a list of things to photograph. Now I would advise leaving some time unplanned. A decorated pole makes a lovely picture, but the invitations to dance, sit down, or pass a plate explained more about this particular holiday. If you come next year, bring your camera and leave yourself time to put it away. Love, Eva
q: Which title would best suit Eva's account?
choices: A Holiday Viewed Through a Camera
A Guide to Preparing a Family Feast
The Demands of a Public Dance Performance

How cloth patterns express Japanese traditions.

Review: A small screen, a large adventure. Yesterday's shadow play at the arts center needed no changing scenery to carry us from a village to a mountain. Behind a cloth screen, performers moved colored leather figures with rods while musicians accompanied the action. Light from behind made the figures visible to us. Their flat bodies seemed an unlikely starting point for such lively characters.
The strongest scene concerned a traveler waiting outside a locked gate. The figure hardly moved, yet the voice grew increasingly impatient. When a drumbeat finally sounded, the gate opened and the traveler jumped back. The musicians were doing more than filling a quiet background: the beat marked the event that changed the character's situation. Movement, voice, and music gave force to a simple visual arrangement.
The ending was less successful. Two minor characters entered, offered advice, and disappeared before I understood why they mattered. The fast pace that made the journey exciting now made its conclusion difficult to follow. A little more time for those exchanges would have helped; more elaborate scenery would not have solved the problem.
A demonstration after the show gave weight to my admiration for the earlier scenes. A performer invited us behind the screen and moved a figure with several separate rods. When a volunteer tried, the figure's legs pulled in different directions. On the audience side, we had seen a traveler taking a confident step. On the other side lay the coordination that made that small step convincing. I left appreciating both the adventure and the practiced hands that had carried it.
q: Which judgment best matches the review as a whole?
choices: The music was effective despite lifeless characters.
The complex scenery distracted from a clear ending.
The acting was skilled, though the ending felt rushed.
The simple figures made the whole journey confusing.

At our school's international welcome event, every guest was asked to choose a short English name. The organizers hoped this would make introductions easier. Some guests welcomed the suggestion; others already had names they wanted classmates to learn. A friendly introduction should make conversation possible, but it should also leave people some control over how they are addressed.
A new name can be a useful choice. One visitor told me that she enjoyed using different names in different languages. To her, the English name was a way to play with language, not a rejection of her family. Another guest said that hearing classmates gradually learn his name made him feel recognized. These reactions are different, but neither needs to become a rule for the other person.
Instead of assigning names, we could ask guests to write the name they prefer on a card and say it aloud. A host could repeat it and ask for correction. This would let each guest guide the introduction. Getting a name right may take several attempts. The effort should not become a performance in which a guest is required to praise every attempt, nor should fear of mistakes prevent a host from trying.
It would be equally unhelpful to impose a ban on English names in the name of cultural respect. That would remove a choice some guests enjoy. The useful question is not which kind of name is more authentic. It is who gets to decide. We should spend less energy choosing names for visitors and more energy listening to the names they choose.
q: What change does the writer principally argue for?
choices: Making short English names compulsory at events.
Having hosts shorten names to avoid speaking errors.
Requiring family names as a sign of cultural respect.
Letting guests decide how they wish to be addressed.
explain: 第二段呈現不同偏好，末段反對強禁英文名，核心是由本人決定。address＝稱呼；強制本名看似尊重文化，仍剝奪選擇。

Dear Lucy, You asked why our holiday album contains so many photographs of the same small town. Before leaving, I had planned to visit five towns in six days. Each had a famous building that I wanted to see. Then I noticed how much of each day would be spent packing, finding a station, and waiting for the next connection. We chose one town as our base, although I worried that we had settled for a less interesting holiday.
On the first morning, we followed the visitor trail and photographed the buildings on our list. By lunchtime, we seemed to have finished the town. The following day, however, we returned to the market without a plan. A seller recognized us and explained why some stalls were empty: several growers were taking a rest after the harvest. Later in the week, those stalls filled again. An empty square that had looked disappointing became part of a story we could follow.
We still missed some sights in the other towns. I would not recommend this arrangement to someone whose main pleasure is comparing famous buildings. For us, though, returning to familiar streets made small changes easier to notice. Our album may look repetitive, but the photographs remind us of different conversations and discoveries. Next time, I will leave room in the plan for a place to become familiar. Love, Emma

Seeing More by Staying in One Place
A Market That Changes with the Harvest
An Easier Way to Travel Between Towns

Notice for visitors to North Reach Island. The narrow road connecting our island to the mainland is covered by the sea at high tide. Island attractions and the road therefore operate on different schedules. A museum ticket shows when you may enter the museum; it does not show when you can reach the island. Before reserving an activity, consult the crossing periods published by the island office for your travel date.
Those periods apply to vehicles using the road. They are not instructions for walking across the surrounding sand, where channels may still contain water. Walkers should use the guided shore walk, which starts and ends on the mainland. Drivers must allow for time on the island as well as the return crossing. A road that is open on arrival may be closed when a late lunch ends. A clear sky does not extend a published crossing period.
Our visitor office provides printed information because phone service is unreliable along parts of the coast. Check for updates before leaving the mainland, and follow any closure signs at the road. If the available crossing period is too short for your intended visit, choose another date or book an overnight stay. Rooms are limited, so do not assume that one will be available if you miss the return crossing. The island is worth exploring, but a successful visit begins with a journey that can be completed as planned.
q: What is the main aim of this notice?

To encourage visitors to stay after the museum closes
To compare island visits with guided mainland walks

A reusable cup is often presented as an environmental answer that you can carry in a bag. The idea has value, but buying such a cup is only the beginning. A cupboard full of unused travel cups does little to reduce the number of throwaway cups used outside the home. To judge a cup fairly, we need to consider its whole life, including how it is made, used, washed, and eventually thrown away.
A strong cup may require more material and energy to produce than a light cup designed for one drink. Repeated use can spread that initial cost over many drinks. This does not mean the cup becomes harmless after a particular number of uses. Washing still uses water and sometimes energy for heating it. The result also depends on what the reusable cup replaces. A cup used frequently for years is a different case from one bought for a single school event and then forgotten.
The practical response is not to search endlessly for the perfect material. If you already own a suitable cup, making it part of your routine may matter more than buying another with a greener label. Schools can help by providing convenient places for cups to be cleaned and kept. Counting how many cups are distributed is easy; finding out whether students keep using them is more useful. An environmental promise becomes meaningful through repeated behavior, rather than through the purchase alone.

choices: Stronger Materials Make Better Travel Cups

Washing Methods Determine a Cup's Full Impact
Greener Cups Depend on Everyday Habits

Matching outdoor light to actual needs
Setting longer hours for use of the field

Stop beside the display of a ship's food supplies. Dried food could last through a long voyage, yet a full stomach did not guarantee good health. Sailors sometimes became weak and developed bleeding gums during months at sea. They were suffering from scurvy, a disease we now link to a lack of vitamin C. Long before vitamins were identified, some sailors had noticed that fresh fruit could help. Knowing a useful practice, however, was different from having a clear explanation for it.
In 1747, the ship's surgeon James Lind compared treatments among twelve sailors with scurvy. According to his account, the men shared a basic diet, but each pair received a different addition. One pair was given oranges and lemons; other pairs received treatments such as vinegar or seawater. The fruit pair improved most clearly. The comparison is remembered because Lind tested several proposed treatments alongside one another instead of relying on a single patient's story.
Do not mistake the fruit in this case for a symbol of an instant solution. Lind had not identified vitamin C, and his report did not lead immediately to routine supplies of citrus juice throughout the British navy. The experiment, published account, and later changes in naval practice belong to different moments. As you move to the next display, consider the distance between observing an improvement and turning that observation into a dependable system. Medical progress includes both learning what helps and making that help regularly available.
q: Which statement best captures the guide's message?
choices: Useful treatment begins with a scientific explanation.
A successful trial brings rapid changes in daily care.
Useful findings require effort to become regular care.
Food supplies matter mainly because of their quantity.
explain: 首段區分經驗與解釋，中段寫比較試驗，末段談供應制度。regular＝經常的；有效療法可早於科學解釋，且試驗不會立即普及照護。

Summer review: Linden Hall cooling room. For two weeks of unusually hot weather, our town opened an air-conditioned room at Linden Hall to residents who needed a cooler place to rest. Entry was free, and no identification was required. Notices appeared on the town website. Staff expected demand to be high, so the small number of visitors during the first three days came as a surprise.
We then spoke to residents in nearby housing blocks. Several knew about the room but believed it was reserved for people receiving emergency aid. Others could not walk to the hall comfortably in the heat. One older resident had seen the web notice but was unsure whether she could bring her grandchild. These responses showed that publishing an address and opening hours had left important questions unanswered. An empty chair did not necessarily mean that nobody needed it.
For the second week, the town arranged a small bus from the housing blocks and placed notices in shops. The new message stated that visitors of different ages were welcome and that they did not have to be receiving emergency aid. Attendance increased, and staff recorded how visitors had learned about the service and reached it. That information will help shape next summer's arrangements. The higher count does not by itself show how many illnesses were prevented. It does, however, suggest that reviewing access and explaining the service more clearly were worthwhile steps. Future planning should examine the journey to a cooling room as carefully as the room itself.
q: How does the report develop its discussion?

It explains how stricter entry rules raised attendance.
It lists changes, then calculates their effects on illness.
It traces low use, explores causes, then reviews changes.

A loaf can become unpleasantly hard even inside a closed bag. This puzzles people who think bread goes stale simply because it loses water to the air. Wrapping certainly limits water loss, but bread can change without becoming much lighter. Something inside the loaf is changing as well.
Much of a loaf consists of starch, a substance also found in rice and potatoes. Baking allows starch to take up water. As the bread cools and ages, parts of the starch gradually arrange themselves into more ordered structures. These changes make the soft middle firmer. Water can also move between different parts of the loaf. Therefore, adding a better wrapper does not remove every cause of staling.
Temperature matters, but colder does not always mean softer for longer. Ordinary refrigerator temperatures can speed up the changes in starch, even though refrigeration slows the growth of mold, a living growth that causes food to decay. Freezing has a different effect: it greatly slows staling. Bread wrapped and frozen while still fresh can therefore keep a pleasant texture longer than bread kept in a refrigerator.
Brief heating can soften bread that has gone stale, but this improvement is temporary. As the loaf cools again, the changes return. Storage decisions thus involve different goals. A method that delays mold may still allow the bread to lose its soft texture. Understanding that difference explains why a loaf can be protected in one way while becoming less enjoyable in another.
q: Which heading best covers the explanation?
choices: How Wrapping Keeps Bread from Drying Out
Why Cold Storage Slows Bread's Decay
explain: 全文說明澱粉、溫度與回熱如何影響麵包變硬。stale（不新鮮的、變硬的）不只涉及失水；包裝防乾只是切入點，不能涵蓋全文。

Student: At your farm, I noticed a small clip around a young tomato stem. Are you repairing a broken plant? Grower: We are joining parts of two living plants. The process is called grafting. The lower plant provides the roots, while the upper part produces the fruit we want to sell. The clip holds the cut surfaces together while they heal. The two parts then grow as a single plant.
Student: Why not grow that upper variety by itself? Grower: Customers like its tomatoes, but certain diseases in our soil can damage its roots. We can attach its stem to roots from a variety selected for resistance to those diseases. This gives us a way to keep growing a popular tomato in a difficult field. It does not mean that every problem disappears; the plants still need suitable water and care.

In a field with serious root disease, fewer lost plants may cover that expense. Where healthy plants already grow well, the extra cost may bring little benefit. We compare small areas before making a larger investment. The comparison includes both the amount of fruit and the money spent producing it.
Student: So the same plant is not the best choice everywhere? Grower: Exactly. A useful farming tool is valuable when it solves a problem that a particular grower actually has.
q: What is the central concern of this interview?
choices: How joining plants lowers the cost of labor.
Why tomato buyers should choose new varieties.
How joining plants can address a field problem.
Why clips are the key to preventing root disease.

Inge Lehmann could not travel to the place she wanted to study. It lay thousands of kilometers beneath her feet. The Danish scientist instead examined records of earthquakes, using waves that traveled through Earth to learn about its hidden interior. Her work shows how an unexpected signal can change a familiar scientific picture.
After a powerful earthquake near New Zealand in 1929, instruments at distant stations recorded waves passing through the planet. According to the accepted model, Earth had a liquid core, or central region, surrounded by solid layers. That model predicted a zone where certain earthquake waves would not be received directly. Yet some stations detected signals where the model suggested they should be absent.
Lehmann compared the records and considered another explanation. Perhaps the core contained a separate inner region that could redirect some waves into the unexpected locations. Fosbury began developing his unusual style while attending high school in Oregon. Instead of crossing the bar with his body facing downward, as many competitors did, he turned his back toward it. His success was the result of development over several years, rather than a sudden choice on the day of the final.

Three pages were carrying one uncertain estimate, and none had obtained a separate decision from the town.

This introductory offer is for residents who want to sample our program before deciding whether regular membership suits them. Each pass provides two admission credits for standard screenings within six weeks of the date it is issued. No membership fee is charged during that period.
A credit can be exchanged for one seat at an eligible screening. Book online or at our desk before attending; holding a pass does not reserve a seat. Standard screenings include a short introduction and a discussion afterward. Special premieres and visiting-director events require separate tickets and cannot be booked with Explorer credits. The calendar identifies these events so that you can check before choosing a film.
Plans can change. Cancel a booking by noon on the day before a screening, and the credit will return to your pass. Later cancellations use up the credit, even if you do not attend. Credits expire when the six-week period ends, so a cancellation does not extend the pass. We recommend checking both the film date and your pass's final date when making a new booking.
After your trial, we will email information about membership. Your account will not become a paid membership unless you choose a plan and confirm payment. The Explorer Pass is a chance to discover whether our films and discussions belong in your routine. It provides a taste of our standard program while leaving the longer-term decision with you.
q: What happens if a resident cancels a Friday screening on Thursday evening?
choices: The credit is used up despite the cancellation.
The credit returns because the screening is a day away.
The credit returns with a later date of expiration.
The credit can be moved to a visiting-director event.
explain: 週五場次須在週四 noon（中午）前取消才退點；週四晚間已逾期，因此點數會用掉。不是只要仍在放映前一天就符合期限。

subject: english
passage:
Dear Editor, your shopping page recently praised a bag advertised as "made in our town." I visited the workshop because I wanted to understand the claim. The workers cut the cloth, sew the pieces, and attach the handles there. Their skill deserves recognition. However, a sentence in your review also described the bag as "local from beginning to end." That was a broader claim than the workshop itself had made.
The owner explained that the cloth comes from another region and the metal parts are bought through a supplier who serves several countries. She showed me records of the sewing work but could not trace every material back to its original producer. This does not make the workers' contribution less real. It does mean that the place where a product is assembled and the origin of its materials are separate questions.
Some buyers may care most about supporting jobs nearby. Others may want to know how far the materials traveled. Both concerns deserve useful information, and the same short label may not answer both. A review that treats local assembly as proof of local materials prevents readers from judging the product by their own priorities.
Please keep reporting on skilled workers in our town, but describe exactly which stages happen here. Where information is unavailable, say so. I would welcome a follow-up that asks suppliers about material origins rather than repeating a wider promise the evidence cannot yet support. Sincerely, Rita
q: Which view best describes Rita's attitude toward local production?
choices: Positive about the work but wanting clear claims.
Doubtful of skills but content with the records.
Sure that local assembly means local materials.
Against town workshops that buy outside materials.
explain: 開頭肯定工人的 skill（技術），結尾也請媒體繼續報導，但要求說清組裝與材料來源；這是支持在地工作並要求準確標示，不是反對外地材料。

subject: english
passage:
On my first Saturday at the animal shelter, I was certain that being a good volunteer meant making friends with every dog. I brought treats, learned their names, and looked forward to long walks. The notebook beside the door seemed like unnecessary paperwork. Experienced volunteers filled it in after each shift, although they could have spent those minutes playing with the animals.
Then I took Milo out. At a corner, he stopped and stared toward a narrow lane. I wrote that he was frightened of traffic. The following week, another volunteer told me Milo had walked happily along the busy road but had stopped at the same corner. Our descriptions seemed to concern different dogs.
A staff member joined our next walk. Instead of pulling Milo onward, she asked what had happened just before he stopped. We checked earlier entries and discovered that his usual walker had taken the lane to a small garden. When we turned that way, Milo immediately moved forward. I had jumped to conclusions about his fear without recording where he had looked.
I still enjoy greeting the dogs, but now I also note the route, the time, and what each animal actually does. An entry such as "waited at the corner and looked left" gives the next person something to check. The notebook lets people on separate shifts build a fuller picture together. My afternoon ends when I close it, but another volunteer's afternoon begins with what I leave behind.
q: Which title best captures the narrator's experience?
choices: Finding a Calmer Route for a Nervous Dog
Replacing Shelter Records with Personal Care
From Dog Walking to Shared Understanding
Letting Dogs Choose Their Daily Activities
explain: 敘事者從只想陪狗，轉為記錄行為並與志工分享理解；observation（觀察）串起前後變化。「替緊張的狗找安靜路線」沿用他最初怕車的誤判，未涵蓋全文。

subject: english
passage:
A town that lets residents vote on public spending appears to be giving everyone an equal voice. Yet a ballot is only the final part of participation. If people cannot help shape the choices printed on it, an open vote may still reflect a narrow range of needs.
Consider a town preparing to spend a small fund on one local project. Ideas were first collected at an evening meeting. Most speakers wanted a sports court, while a proposal for lights along a footpath received little attention. Later, paper forms placed at bus stops revealed another view. Several early-shift workers used that path before sunrise but could not attend the meeting. Their absence had hidden a need, not removed it.
This does not prove that the lights deserve to win. The sports court may benefit more residents, and both plans require estimates of building and future repair costs. What matters is that a proposal should carry weight because of the need it addresses and the evidence supporting it, rather than the number of confident speeches made for it.
Before holding the vote, the town should publish a short comparison of the proposals and invite comments through more than one channel. Afterward, it should explain how the chosen project will be checked. Residents need a fair chance to question a plan as well as support one. Participation becomes meaningful when the town listens before the ballot and remains responsible after it.
q: Which statement best expresses the writer's position?
choices: Public meetings best reveal the town's main needs.
A plan merits support when more people request it.
Written proposals deserve priority in the town vote.
Fair participation extends beyond voting day.
explain: 首段重視選項如何形成，末段要求投票前傾聽、投票後負責；participation（參與）不限投票。書面管道是補足缺席者的聲音，並非優先權。

subject: english
passage:
Reporter: Your neighborhood exchange uses hours instead of money. How does that work? Coordinator: A member earns one credit by helping another member for an hour. The helper may later spend that credit on help from someone else. Last week, Ana helped Ben practice a presentation. Ben repaired a shelf for Jo, who showed Ana how to use a sewing machine. Nobody had to return the exact service they received.
Reporter: Does every hour have the same value? Coordinator: In our exchange, yes. We are not trying to copy the prices of professional services. Equal credits recognize that everyone's time matters. But members still agree on the task beforehand. An hour of sewing instruction does not include the cost of cloth, and members should not accept jobs requiring qualifications they lack.
Reporter: What surprised you after the exchange began? Coordinator: Some members kept earning credits but rarely requested help. They liked being useful and felt uncomfortable becoming receivers. A large balance in an account looked like success, yet it meant that the help was not circulating. We began asking new members to name something they wanted to learn, not simply something they could offer.
Reporter: Has that changed the way you judge the project? Coordinator: Yes. We still record the hours, but we also ask whether members feel able to request assistance. The exchange works best when people can contribute in one situation and receive in another. Collecting credits is a means of connecting neighbors, not our final goal.
q: What is the exchange chiefly intended to encourage?
choices: Building ties through giving and receiving
Giving skilled services their usual market value
Helping members build up large credit balances
Pairing neighbors who can return the same service
explain: 末段說連結鄰里才是目標，付出與求助都重要；contribute（貢獻）。大量點數若未使用，反而表示協助未流通，並非越存越好。

An airport is usually a gateway for travelers. In western Berlin in 1948, however, airports became a way to keep a city supplied. Food and fuel arrived by air because the usual connections with the outside world had been cut.
After World War II, Germany was divided into zones controlled by the victorious powers. Berlin was also divided, although the city lay within the Soviet-controlled part of Germany. In June 1948, Soviet authorities blocked road, rail, and water routes to western Berlin. Britain and the United States responded by flying in supplies. This was more than a matter of sending a few planes with emergency food. A city needed regular deliveries, and fuel was essential for keeping homes warm as winter approached. Crews on the ground had to unload cargo so that planes could return for another load. To sustain the operation, flights had to become part of a dependable system.
The blockade ended in May 1949, but the airlift did not erase the wider division between the Soviet Union and the Western powers. Its importance lay in a more immediate achievement: access by land had been denied, yet the city continued to receive supplies. Aircraft became tools for supporting daily life during a political struggle, rather than simply carrying people across long distances.

How aircraft maintained supplies during a political crisis
How Berlin replaced its airports with land routes
How fuel shortages caused Berlin's division after the war

subject: english

Welcome to the gallery "Fields That Remember." The objects discussed here are not displayed in glass cases. Many remain underground. Archaeologists, researchers who study past human life, can sometimes locate them by studying the crops growing above them. Our subject is the hidden connection between plant growth and buried traces of human activity.
A stone wall under a field can leave a thinner layer of soil for roots. Plants above it may grow less strongly than the surrounding crop. An old ditch can have the opposite effect. After it fills with soil and other material, it may hold more moisture than the ground around it, allowing plants above it to grow taller. In dry conditions, such differences can become easier to notice.
The resulting patterns are called crop marks. A line of weaker plants might follow a buried wall; a ring of taller plants might follow an old ditch. From ground level, a visitor may see scattered changes without recognizing a pattern. Seen from above, the same changes can suggest the outline of a vanished structure. Researchers can then decide where further investigation would be useful.
However, a clear shape does not automatically identify an ancient building. Modern drains and farming practices can also affect crop growth. Nor does an unmarked field prove that nothing lies beneath it: not every buried feature produces a visible change. The field offers clues rather than a complete account. Reading those clues means combining them with other evidence, not treating an attractive pattern as a finished discovery.
q: What is the gallery text designed to explain?
choices: How dry weather improves the growth of field crops
How buried stone walls provide moisture for plants
How crop patterns offer clues to underground remains
How crop marks identify the age of ancient buildings
explain: 全文介紹作物生長與地下遺跡的關聯，並提醒判讀限制；clue（線索）。文章未教人用痕跡測定建築年代，不能把發現線索擴大成定年。

Harbor District Tsunami Walk: Public Practice Notice
Join our guided walk from the fishing square to Hill School this Sunday at nine. The event is a practice, not a response to an actual warning. It is open to residents and visitors, including people who do not normally join neighborhood activities. Please wear comfortable shoes and bring water.
At the square, the leader will explain natural warning signs, such as a strong or long earthquake near the coast or a sudden unusual change in sea level. These signs can mean that a tsunami is possible. In a real event, people in a low coastal area should move toward higher ground or inland as soon as they can safely do so, without waiting for a phone message to confirm the danger. If the ground is shaking, protect yourself first and move once the shaking stops.
During Sunday's walk, follow the leader along the marked route. At two crossings, volunteers will ask participants to point out the next sign before continuing. This is not a race. We want to discover which directions are hard to follow, particularly for someone seeing them for the first time. Please tell us afterward if a sign was hidden or confusing.
The practice will finish at Hill School. Finishing the walk does not mean that people could return immediately during a real tsunami. Dangerous waves can continue after the first one, and participants should learn to wait until local authorities have cleared the area for return. Sunday's discussion will therefore cover both reaching safety and knowing when to leave it.
q: What is the notice's main purpose?
choices: To test alerts before reopening a coastal route
To train guides to lead a faster walk to school
To prepare visitors to assess sea conditions
To practice escape and improve route guidance
explain: 活動兼具練習避難與蒐集指標回饋的目的；evacuation（疏散）。介紹自然警訊不等於要參加者評估海況，辨認路標才是沿途任務。

Dear Lina,
You asked why our riverside market closed yesterday when the sky above town was blue. I wondered the same thing. The sellers had already put out their tables, and a few visitors complained that the flood warning must have been a mistake. From the bridge, the river still looked ordinary.
Later, our science teacher explained what we had missed. A river carries water from a much larger area than the stretch we can see. Heavy rain had fallen in the hills upstream. That water was moving toward town, even though the storm itself had stayed far away. The local sky told us about the weather over our heads, not about everything entering the river. A warning could therefore arrive before an obvious change in the water beside the market.
By afternoon, the riverside path was underwater. I was glad the stalls had been packed up earlier, but my father reminded me that the decision did not need that later scene to be reasonable. Waiting to see water on the path would have left much less time to move people and equipment. The warning was useful because it allowed action while the place still looked safe.
I used to think a remote storm was someone else's problem. Now I would ask where its water might go. Next time you visit, we can choose a cafe on the higher street if the river area is closed. The view is less dramatic, but I no longer need a dramatic view to believe a warning.
Love,
Mia
q: What is Mia chiefly explaining to Lina?
choices: Why closing the market on a sunny day made sense
Why sellers moved the market permanently uphill
Why afternoon flooding made earlier alerts unnecessary
Why the forecast failed to predict rain above the town

Review of the North Hall Earthquake Practice
The hall's first drill report looked encouraging: everyone on the attendance list reached the outdoor meeting area, and the final group arrived within the planned time. The review team, however, was asked to examine how the result had been achieved, not merely record the total.
Participants first practiced protecting themselves during shaking. After the practice signal ended, staff directed them along the agreed exit routes. Most followed spoken instructions. Two visitors who could not hear the announcements moved only after seeing others leave. Neither knew which outdoor area had been chosen, so a quick arrival did not necessarily show that the instructions had reached them. In the written survey, one visitor said she had followed a familiar face rather than a direction.
Another difficulty appeared when a volunteer who normally checked the side room was absent. A second volunteer eventually checked it, but only after noticing that the task had no name beside it on the duty sheet. The room was empty. This fortunate result did not show that the checking procedure was dependable. The original report did not account for the delay before someone took over the absent volunteer's task.
The team recommended visible messages alongside announcements and a named substitute for each checking duty. At the next practice, observers will record whether people receive directions independently and whether tasks transfer when someone is missing. Arrival time will still be recorded. It will be considered together with evidence that the procedure can work with different people, rather than treated as a complete measure of readiness.
q: Which heading best reflects the review team's conclusion?
choices: Faster Arrival Should Guide the Next Practice
A Good Result Can Hide Weak Emergency Procedures
Following Familiar People Makes Instructions Clear
An Empty Room Shows That Checking Duties Work
explain: 全員及時到達卻未必收到指示，空房也未證明查房可靠；procedure（流程）。「空房表示查房有效」把幸運結果誤當流程證據。

subject: english
passage:
Review of the North Hall Earthquake Practice
The hall's first drill report looked encouraging: everyone on the attendance list reached the outdoor meeting area, and the final group arrived within the planned time. The review team, however, was asked to examine how the result had been achieved, not merely record the total.
Participants first practiced protecting themselves during shaking. After the practice signal ended, staff directed them along the agreed exit routes. Most followed spoken instructions. Two visitors who could not hear the announcements moved only after seeing others leave. Neither knew which outdoor area had been chosen, so a quick arrival did not necessarily show that the instructions had reached them. In the written survey, one visitor said she had followed a familiar face rather than a direction.
Another difficulty appeared when a volunteer who normally checked the side room was absent. A second volunteer eventually checked it, but only after noticing that the task had no name beside it on the duty sheet. The room was empty. This fortunate result did not show that the checking procedure was dependable. The original report did not account for the delay before someone took over the absent volunteer's task.
The team recommended visible messages alongside announcements and a named substitute for each checking duty. At the next practice, observers will record whether people receive directions independently and whether tasks transfer when someone is missing. Arrival time will still be recorded. It will be considered together with evidence that the procedure can work with different people, rather than treated as a complete measure of readiness.
q: How do the visitor and side-room examples work together?
choices: They show how delays identify the slowest participants.
They link both problems to the absent volunteer.
They compare two ways of counting those who arrive.
They expose problems that the arrival figures leave out.
explain: 訪客靠跟人、查房靠臨時補位，兩例顯示到達數字無法呈現流程弱點；figure（數字）。缺席志工只與查房有關，不能解釋訪客沒聽到指示。
