subject: english
passage:
Two desk lamps in a design classroom looked almost identical. When a wire broke inside each one, students discovered a hidden difference. One lamp could be opened with a standard screwdriver; the other had a cover fixed permanently with glue.
The teacher asked students to record each step of reaching the wire. Students working on the screwed cover removed four screws and lifted it off. The other group had to cut the glued cover, damaging its edge. The task showed that access to an internal part can determine whether an otherwise simple repair is practical.
A second factor concerned component connections. In one model, the wire could be unplugged and replaced separately. In the other, it was permanently joined to a larger unit. Replacing that single wire therefore required changing several working components too. This raised costs despite equally small faults. Both lamps had sold for the same price, so the difference could not be explained by one being a cheaper purchase.
The final factor was information. A diagram beside the workbench showed the order in which parts should be removed. A group given the diagram completed the disassembly sooner than a group using an identical lamp without it. After recording the time taken to remove the parts, the students ended the comparison. Neither group switched on its lamp after putting it back together.
The teacher's conclusion was that products carry hidden decisions about their future. Access, component connections, and clear instructions together shape what happens after something goes wrong. A tidy exterior may attract a buyer, but it reveals little about whether that buyer will later be able to replace a broken part.
q: Which title best covers the discussion?
choices: The Hidden Design Choices That Affect Repairs
How Classroom Trials Measure Lamp Performance
The Role of Purchase Price in Repair Costs
Why Repair Instructions Matter More than Access
explain: 全文以開啟方式、零件連接及說明資訊，說明隱藏設計如何影響維修；不是測試燈具性能或只談售價，也未說說明書比開啟方式更重要。

Faster work did not establish a successful repair.
The diagram prevented damage to working parts.
The slower group faced a more complicated fault.

Borrowing rules at the imaginary Lark Film Archive changed several times. An argument over access began when a student filmmaker was refused a historic camera even though she had completed a training course.
[1] The archive's original 1998 policy reserved every camera for paid staff. In 2005, a student named Mira published a complaint under the pen name "Reelbird," because she wanted readers to focus on the policy rather than her identity. [2] The complaint prompted a review, and a new borrowing system took effect in 2007. Applicants first had to complete training; training alone did not guarantee approval.
The 2007 system divided equipment into three categories. Basic cameras were available to trained members for projects of any length. Advanced cameras required both training and a project lasting no more than fourteen days. Historic cameras remained restricted to staff, regardless of project length. [3] Supporters praised the wider access, while critics said the historic collection was still too difficult to study.
In 2016, the archive added a separate six-day limit for every camera borrowed for an off-campus project. That restriction operated alongside the category rules. A trained member could therefore use an advanced camera off campus for six days, but not for ten. Basic cameras were also subject to the off-campus limit.
[4] In 2020, a donor offered replacement cameras. The archive then opened historic models to trained students for on-campus projects lasting at most three days. The donation also expanded the supply of basic cameras. No later changes are covered here.
q: Which expression in paragraph two refers to a name used to conceal a writer's identity?
explain: Mira 以 Reelbird 發表而不公開身分，pen name 指「筆名」；identity 是身分，complaint 是抱怨或申訴。

subject: english
passage:
Sound designer Nela grew up above her aunt's clock repair shop in an imagined town. Customers brought clocks that clicked, rang, or fell silent. Nela learned to distinguish tiny mechanical noises long before she studied music. When a burst pipe closed the shop temporarily, she recorded nearby workplaces to preserve their familiar sounds.
At college, she was urged to compose for concert halls. She instead became interested in the unnoticed rhythms of everyday labor. She disliked performances that kept listeners far from sound makers. Her projects placed listeners close to workers' movements. She described her approach this way: "A small repeated noise tells me where to begin; I follow the hands that made it." Her childhood listening habits became a method of composition.
One installation, called Closing Time, filled a dark room with the sounds of a night bakery. Visitors heard trays sliding, a brush sweeping flour, and a latch closing. The recordings were arranged in a slow circle, so that each sound seemed to pass to another worker. On the central wall, three pale handprints appeared above a low horizontal strip of light. No faces or complete bodies were shown. The prints represented people whose work was visible although their identities went unnoticed. The light suggested the narrow opening used for bread deliveries before sunrise.
Nela's work did not attempt to recreate an entire bakery. She left out conversations with customers and the sound of money changing hands. These omissions kept attention on preparation rather than sales. Local apprentices later began recording other workplaces. Nela welcomed their choices, encouraging new questions rather than copies.
q: Which title best captures the passage?
choices: How Sound Art Preserved an Entire Town's Working History
From Clock Repairs to a Career in Concert Music
How Visitors Helped Design a Bakery Sound Project
From Childhood Listening to Art about Working Hands
explain: 全文串連童年聆聽經驗、創作理念及作品，重點是聆聽如何成為藝術；working hands 指勞動者。

An imagined workshop examined interruptions and students' ability to follow a sequence. Students often checked messages while assembling classroom models. A finished model could look convincing even when a hidden step had been skipped.
For the workshop, forty volunteers first completed a questionnaire about their usual work habits, including how often they switched away from an unfinished task. The instructors then showed each volunteer a sequence of twelve simple folding actions. After watching, volunteers sorted pictures of those actions into two categories: actions requiring a tool and actions done by hand. Pressing a fold with a ruler counted as tool use; folding with fingers did not. This encouraged close examination of the actions.
Following an eight-minute break, volunteers received a new picture set containing both familiar and unfamiliar actions. They indicated which actions had appeared earlier and placed the familiar ones in the remembered order. Meanwhile, a camera recorded how often their eyes left the work area, and a simple counter recorded unplanned pauses. Frequent glances away or unexpected stops could indicate that attention had shifted from the sequence.
Volunteers reporting frequent task switching tended to omit more actions. However, the workshop did not assign their everyday habits, and other differences between volunteers might have contributed to the pattern. The instructors therefore avoided claiming that checking messages caused the errors. They suggested trying a quiet work period and then comparing performance. Their report emphasized the possible cost of interrupted attention while leaving room for a more carefully controlled test.
q: Which aim best describes this report?

To explain why picture classification prevents later errors.
To recommend a proven routine for limiting message use.
To examine a possible link between interruptions and errors.
explain: 文章以工作坊檢視注意力中斷與漏步驟的關聯；possible link 是「可能的關聯」，非確立因果。

subject: english

In the fictional town of Millhaven, residents can now renew library cards and reserve public rooms through a single website. Town officials call this a service improvement: people no longer need to visit several offices during working hours. Yet local volunteers have noticed a less obvious result. The gap does not simply divide people who own computers from those who do not. An older resident may have a phone but struggle to read small instructions. A parent may understand the forms but share one device with three children. Someone using a prepaid connection may avoid downloading large documents because doing so consumes the data needed for work.
Digital services nevertheless offer real advantages. Applications can be processed more quickly, and residents can check their progress without making repeated journeys. Staff spend less time copying details and more time answering difficult questions.
The difficulty is that savings for an office do not automatically produce equal access for residents. Closing a help desk before people can use its digital replacement may leave those with limited skills or equipment dependent on neighbors. A cheaper system on paper can therefore shift effort onto households least able to spare it.
The town is now testing shorter forms with residents who use different devices. Volunteers will record where users stop and ask for help. Officials plan to compare these observations with the processing times reported by staff before deciding which service counters to retain.

choices: Explain a hidden difficulty in moving services online.

Attribute the access gap to rising office expenses.

subject: english
passage:
Imagine telling a joke to a friend and then hearing it repeated at a formal meeting. The words remain the same, but the audience changes their meaning. A similar problem can occur online when material created for one circle reaches several different audiences. This is described as a collapse of context.
In a small group, people rely on shared knowledge. When a message moves beyond that group, those clues may disappear. Readers can interpret the words literally, attach a different purpose to them, or judge the speaker by standards that were never part of the original exchange.
Consider a volunteer who posts a humorous complaint about a rainy cleanup day in a private chat. Her friends know she stayed until the work was finished. A screenshot shared on a public noticeboard, however, may make her appear unwilling to help. Similarly, a photograph of a child's awkward first attempt at dancing might delight relatives but embarrass the child when circulated among classmates. Neither the volunteer's completed work nor the child's effort has changed; only the people viewing the material have.
Responsible sharing differs from this casual forwarding. It involves asking the speaker before expanding the audience and supplying enough background for new readers to understand the message.
There is no simple test that predicts every misunderstanding. Even permission cannot guarantee that readers will respond as expected. Still, before forwarding a message, we can ask whose words we are moving, where they are going, and what background will be lost. Treating access to a message as a reason to pause, rather than automatic permission to distribute it, helps protect trust.
q: Which statement best captures the passage?
choices: Falsehoods are the main cause of online confusion.
Screenshots preserve context for new readers.
Moving messages between audiences requires care.
explain: 文章說明不同受眾間轉傳訊息的風險，並提出負責任的做法；audience 是「受眾」。

Westbridge is a town known for gardens on the roofs of its apartment buildings. The practice began when a local nursery offered residents unwanted seed packets at very low prices. Even tenants with small household budgets could start growing herbs. __1__ Soon, small pots appeared above shops and homes across the town.
Interest declined when several roofs were converted into storage areas. Years later, a long summer of indoor building repairs renewed residents' desire for outdoor meeting places. A tenants' association proposed restoring the gardens, this time with shared equipment and clearer rules.
Initially, the town charged building owners for removing large unwanted items but offered no support for gardening. A later grant helped owners repair roof surfaces before residents added plants. Tenants also contributed a small annual fee for tools. Volunteers, rather than paid town workers, took turns checking the beds and replacing worn labels.
The present gardens share several practical features. Raised beds stand along the edges, leaving a broad central walkway clear. Tool cupboards sit near the entrance so that people do not need to carry equipment through planted areas. Each roof includes a shaded bench at the far end, away from the entrance, where visitors can rest without blocking arriving gardeners. Nothing is planted directly on a roof surface; every bed rests on a protective base.
The gardens developed through changing needs, public support, and residents' work. They are valued not simply for the herbs they produce but for making a once neglected part of each building useful to people with different interests and levels of gardening experience.

choices: Low seed prices made roof-surface repairs unnecessary.
Cheap starting materials helped spread the practice.
The nursery supplied seeds after the later grant began.
The small household budgets paid for the shared tools.

When a hillside fire damaged the water supply of Brook Hollow, several nearby villages organized a joint recovery effort. The fire had left the main storage tank usable, but a broken underground pipe prevented water from reaching homes. The team's immediate objective was to restore that connection before residents exhausted their emergency supplies.
The first survey produced a surprise. A repair company had charged some families for replacing sections of pipe that were still broken. Old payment records showed that the company had accepted fees without completing the promised work. These documents did not explain why the fire had started, but they helped the villages decide which claims needed further investigation.
Working together, the volunteers located a detailed map of the underground network and a set of matching replacement joints in an unused workshop. The map revealed a route that avoided the damaged hillside. Using that route would require permission from two landowners, so village representatives met them while engineers checked the joints. This division of work shortened the delay.
Water began reaching homes again after the new connection passed a pressure test. The organizers credited the result to shared equipment, technical knowledge, and local contacts. They proposed regular meetings among the villages, arguing that relationships built before an emergency could be as valuable as supplies stored for one.
q: What was the recovery team's immediate goal?

To replace the main water storage tank.
To examine the repair company's finances.
To reconnect homes to the water supply.

Bridge begins twenty minutes after Spiral, and its operator pauses between demonstrations to let visitors examine how the blocks connect. Beyond it stands Lantern, the tallest model in the hall. The final display, Wave, begins at 10:30 near the back wall. It consists of parallel metal strips that bend in sequence when a hidden bar turns. From the side, the moving strips resemble a rolling sea. Unlike the other models, Wave contains no wheels or hanging strings visible to the audience.
Volunteers demonstrate the machines repeatedly throughout the afternoon. The opening schedule is most useful for visitors who want to watch the first performance of each display. Visitors can return later to ask about construction details.

Evaluate which club deserves the exhibition prize.
Introduce the designs and operation of four models.

Rita's journal illustrates an approach her workshop calls purposeful making. Members question whether public recognition should be the main measure of a hobby's value. A hand-operated book press holds sheets firmly together while glue dries. At the Alder Book Workshop, presses also flatten folded paper, help attach cloth covers, and straighten pages that have become slightly bent. A press does not replace careful binding, but it applies pressure more evenly than a person can by hand. The workshop's collection shows how changes in a simple tool can alter the work people do.
The oldest model in the collection is a wedge press. It has two broad wooden boards joined loosely by straps. Workers place a book between them and push thin wedges beneath the straps. As the wedges go farther in, the straps tighten and draw the boards together. This model needs neither a screw nor a turning handle, but adjusting pressure precisely is difficult.
A later bench press uses two metal screws, one at each end of the top board. The worker turns a small handle on each screw in turn, lowering the board toward a fixed base. If one side is lowered too far, the book may become uneven. The frame stands on a workbench rather than enclosing a tall storage space.
The workshop's newest model has a single central screw and a sliding upper plate. Metal guides keep the plate level as a large wheel turns the screw. Because workers no longer have to balance two separate screws, they can adjust pressure more quickly. The tall frame also accepts a larger stack of books. However, staff still use the wedge press when demonstrating older techniques. They emphasize that a newer design can make a task easier without making every earlier tool useless. Choosing a press depends on the book, the available space, and the purpose of the work.
q: Which task is NOT listed as a use of the workshop presses?
explain: 文章列出壓平摺紙、固定布封面及整平微彎頁面；printing patterns「印製圖案」未列為用途。

subject: english
passage:
A museum team has found an unusual source of help: routine photographs taken by lighthouse keepers. The museum is studying painted harbor signs that have faded over decades. Its own records show only when each sign entered the collection, leaving long gaps in the history of the colors. Lighthouse pictures are filling those gaps.
The keepers originally photographed the harbor to record visibility conditions. At the start of every morning shift, they took a picture from the same window and noted whether distant buildings could be seen clearly. Their purpose was to document how fog affected the view, not to preserve local art. Yet several painted signs appeared near the edge of each photograph. Because the camera position remained nearly constant, researchers can compare the same sign across many years.
The images are far from perfect. Changing light alters the appearance of paint, and sea spray sometimes leaves marks on the window. The team selects pictures taken under similar conditions and uses objects of known colors for comparison. Researchers look for patterns across dozens of images. They wear gloves when handling the old negatives and make digital copies before attempting any cleaning. Even a digital copy cannot reproduce every detail of the original film.
The museum gives the keepers recognition by displaying their names beside the restored signs. This lets visitors see whose patient work made the project possible. The project cannot recover every original shade, but narrows the likely colors and shows which decisions have strong evidence. The team now asks other harbor offices to check whether similarly useful collections have survived.
q: Which title best covers the passage?
choices: A New Lighthouse for a Foggy Harbor
Why Harbor Artists Prefer Bright Paint
Weather Records Help Recover Faded Art
explain: 全文核心是燈塔的天候照片意外協助修復褪色標誌，跨越照片來源、分析與保存價值；不是介紹新燈塔。

subject: english
passage:
Marlow Map Library holds two versions of a survey atlas. Both are called the River Atlas. An exhibition guide compares their designs, histories, and ownership rules.
The first atlas entered use forty years before its retirement as the official survey record in 1952. Its designer, French mapmaker Elise Moreau, bound the hand-drawn pages in blue cloth. The volume measured 32 centimeters in height and weighed two kilograms. During a flood in 1940, librarian Peter Hall moved it to a dry attic. This rescue later led to the mistaken story that he had designed it. In 1952, the town transferred ownership to the local historical society. The original disappeared from its unlocked display case in 1961 and has never been found. What visitors now see is a copy made from earlier photographs.
A replacement atlas entered service in 1956. Designed by Canadian surveyor Robin Dale, it has a green leather cover and stands 44 centimeters high. The library owns this volume and keeps it in a secure room; no loss or theft of it is recorded. From 1956 onward, a new survey summary was added every eight years, without interruption, through 2020. Each summary occupies one labeled slot, and the volume has twelve slots in total. The first summary was inserted when the atlas entered service.
Under the library's rules, researchers may borrow a printed reproduction for a limited period. Ownership of the original remains permanent, but possession of a reproduction is temporary. The library plans to keep that distinction even after the replacement atlas becomes full. Staff hope the two volumes will encourage visitors to think about how institutions preserve information while still making it available.
q: When did the first River Atlas enter official use?
explain: 第一冊在 1952 年退休，啟用時間早四十年，因此是 1952－40＝1912 年。retirement 指「退休、停止使用」。

subject: english
passage:
Students designed hanging gardens called rain pockets. Each pocket consists of a cloth pouch, a firm frame, and a shallow tray beneath it. Water passes through the cloth slowly, while the tray catches what escapes. The pockets vary from small envelopes holding one seedling to broad panels supporting several plants. They have been installed inside classrooms and on sheltered balconies, but none has been placed along the school's open rooftop path.
A successful pocket requires several conditions. The cloth must allow excess water to drain without letting the planting material fall out. The frame must support the pouch when wet, and the plants must receive suitable light. The tray is emptied after watering, rather than used to keep the pouch standing in water. For outdoor displays, the team selected sites protected from strong wind.
The exhibition notes divide each pocket's history into two stages. During the assembly stage, students fit the frame and pouch together without plants. During the growing stage, the pocket contains living plants and needs regular inspection. A pocket can return to the assembly stage if its cloth must be replaced. These labels describe a display's condition, not a fixed calendar period. Two pockets built on the same day may enter the growing stage several days apart.
The final section explains what the school gains from the project. Classes use the pockets to compare how different planting materials retain moisture. Art students explore patterns across the panels, and a hallway display gives visitors a reason to discuss water use. The pockets thus serve as teaching materials, creative surfaces, and starting points for conversation.
q: Which description matches the exhibition notes?
choices: The trays supply water directly to the planting material.
The pouches use sealed cloth to retain excess water.
The rooftop path is used for the largest garden panels.
The displays come in different sizes and locations.
explain: 第一段指出可小如信封、大如面板，設置於教室和有遮蔽陽臺。vary 是「有差異」。

subject: english
passage:
At a community archive, retired clockmaker Ada volunteers beside a tape-sorting machine. Visitors usually notice the machine first. Ada quietly asks visitors where a recording came from and whose voices they expect to hear.
When the archive opened, Ada's task was simply to repair damaged tape cases. After several months, an assistant noticed something unusual. Ada sometimes set an apparently ordinary tape aside before the machine played it. Those tapes frequently contained rare local performances. She did not claim a special power. A handwritten date, an unfamiliar brand, or the way a label had been attached could suggest a history worth investigating.
The staff began recording her decisions. When she marked a tape for closer study, a researcher checked its ownership history and listened to it. Some choices revealed important recordings; others turned out to be ordinary home material. Ada said the unsuccessful cases mattered because they showed where her judgment needed improvement. The machine, meanwhile, continued to sort the larger collection by recording length.
During preparations for a public exhibition, a visitor heard about the imminent opening and asked whether Ada could identify every valuable tape instantly. She laughed. Years of repair work had taught her to notice clues, not to guarantee results. The staff agreed that her observations were useful precisely when followed by careful checks. They also valued the conversations she began: a visitor who remembered a relative's performance might supply a name that no machine could recover from the tape alone. The archive therefore kept both the quick sorting machine and Ada's slow, questioning table.
q: Which title best captures this account?
choices: Restoring Damaged Tapes for a Public Exhibition
Recording Length as a Guide to Local History
Human Clues and Mechanical Order in an Archive
A Clockmaker Reconstructs Her Family Recordings
explain: 全文主軸是 Ada 透過經驗察覺線索，再經查證，與機器大量排序互補。修理外殼僅是早期任務；錄音長度與家族錄音均非全文重點。

A school logistics club built a tabletop model for moving parcels between desks. Each complete unit is called a station, and it has several components. A belt carries parcels away from the loading point. Between neighboring stations, a bridge supports a parcel while it crosses the space separating the desks. Beyond that space, a tray collects arriving parcels until students remove them. The tray and belt can be replaced separately without replacing the station.
A repair sheet describes three problems without naming the parts. At desk P, a parcel remains beside the loading point although the belt is switched on and the next tray is empty. Between P and Q, another parcel falls into the space between the desks. A third reaches Q successfully but rolls onto the floor before anyone can collect it. Students identify faulty parts before making repairs.
The first version had many decorative towers and extra side routes. To make testing manageable, the club decided to streamline the model: towers disappeared, unused side routes were removed, and essential delivery paths stayed. Students recorded which paths visitors selected. Repeatedly selected paths received clearer labels, while rarely chosen ones remained available for later trials.
One feature stayed separate from these improvements. A safety control stops a belt when the next tray is full. Its warning light takes two seconds to reflect the tray's condition, whereas the decorative lights flash immediately. Thus, a quick flash does not establish that the next desk is ready. In one trial, a visitor followed a quick flash and sent a second parcel before the first was removed. The belt stopped, delaying the delivery.
q: A record names the complete unit whose belt and tray were replaced. Which label belongs on that record?
explain: station 是「整座工作站」；belt 與 tray 可各別更換而不必換整座，因此包含兩者的完整單位是 station。bridge 只是跨桌面的部件。

subject: english
passage:
The public clock in the fictional town of Linden once stood inside a textile factory. Workers checked it before each shift, and apprentices learned to maintain its gears. The manager required every repair to be entered in a large notebook, with the date, the worker's name, and the parts replaced. __1__ The notebook later became an unusually detailed record of daily factory life.
When the factory closed, residents rescued the clock and placed it in the town library. Former employees met beneath it on Sunday afternoons, sharing stories with students who had never seen the factory operating. Families donated photographs, and the library displayed them beside the clock. __2__ However, as the building grew busier, few people paused long enough to read the small labels or understand the clock's connection with local life.
__3__ Rather than moving the clock to a separate museum, the team proposed short recordings played through handsets. Each recording would connect a visible part of the machine with a worker's memory. Visitors could listen while watching the gears move, and quieter hours would be reserved for school groups preparing questions about the factory.
The library approved a trial, but staff still had to record interviews, check permissions, and rewrite unclear descriptions. __4__ Even so, the team believed that helping residents hear one another's memories justified the effort. Its aim was to let a familiar machine open conversations between generations, rather than merely occupy a corner of a crowded room.
q: __1__ 處最適合填入哪一個句子？
choices: A small volunteer team therefore suggested a new way to explain its history.
Completing those tasks would take longer than the team had expected.
That habit made individual repairs traceable many years afterward.
The factory had once produced cloth in several different colors.
The machine had become a meeting point for different generations.
explain: That habit（那個習慣）回指逐次記錄維修；可追查個別修理又銜接後面的詳細生活紀錄。

subject: english
passage:
In a riverside town, a retired tailor named Elena began creating adjustable clothing for children who used wheelchairs. Ordinary jackets often bunched behind their backs, while small buttons were difficult to close. When Elena first displayed her designs at a local fair, several shop owners dismissed them as a hobby with little practical future. They predicted that families would prefer familiar brands to clothing made in a tiny workshop.
Elena had spent years repairing school uniforms, but this project required a different kind of knowledge. She invited families to describe their daily routines and watched, with permission, how children put on coats. A pocket that looked convenient on a standing model could become unreachable when its wearer sat down. She began placing openings along the sides and replacing narrow fasteners with broad fabric tabs.
Progress was slow. For each early fitting, Elena carried a bag containing six versions of the same sleeve. Often none worked well enough, and she returned to her table with more notes than finished garments. The children helped her compare the designs rather than simply accepting what an adult thought they needed. Their comments became a guide for the next round of changes.
Eventually, a school ordered a small collection, and other workshops requested her patterns. Elena shared the drawings and asked makers to keep collecting feedback instead of treating her measurements as permanent rules. Her achievement was more than a new range of clothes: it encouraged designers to build users' experience into the making process. The workshop remained small, but its approach spread far beyond the town.
q: Where would this account most likely appear?
choices: A guide to caring for delicate fabrics
A collection of practical design profiles
A catalog of seasonal clothing discounts
A manual for operating sewing machines
explain: 本文記述一位設計者如何解決使用者的困難，適合實用設計人物故事集（design profiles），並非洗衣指南或商品目錄。

subject: english
passage:
The underground music hall in the imagined town of Bellwick began as an empty water-storage chamber. After a new reservoir replaced it, the chamber stood unused. A local arts group proposed turning it into a place for performances. The project required more than bringing in chairs: narrow entrances, damp walls, and uneven echoes all had to be addressed before audiences could enter.
The construction team recruited workers from a nearby furniture workshop that had recently closed. Their experience in shaping wood proved useful when fitting seats and sound panels into the curved space. Before work began, each person practiced using a safety harness in a training room. Throughout the conversion, nobody suffered an injury serious enough to require hospital treatment.
Several discoveries forced the designers to revise their drawings. A blocked passage could not become the main exit, so they widened a second route. Ordinary wall coverings trapped moisture against the old brick. To solve that problem, the team devised a removable panel with an air space behind it. Test panels were installed for a month before the group ordered enough for the entire hall.
The hall now hosts weekend concerts, but maintaining it is an ongoing task. Every spring, technicians remove selected panels, inspect the brick, and replace any damaged supports. During unusually wet weeks, extra checks are arranged before performances. The arts group publishes these maintenance records so that future caretakers can understand why particular materials were chosen. Visitors tend to notice the music first; behind it lies a less visible history of testing, careful construction, and regular care.
q: Which title best covers the passage?
choices: A Debate over the Cost of Live Music
How to Perform in an Underground Space
A Water Chamber Becomes a Music Hall
explain: 全文從水槽改建的緣起，寫到施工、安全與後續維護，標題須涵蓋 conversion（改建）全程，而非只談演出技巧。

When Hana became director of a regional parcel-delivery cooperative, complaints about lost packages were usually blamed on careless drivers. Supervisors believed that occasional losses were simply the price of moving thousands of items quickly. Yet Hana noticed that many drivers received route changes through hurried telephone calls, while warehouse workers used several incompatible versions of the same address list. She questioned whether individual carelessness explained the pattern.
Supervisors promised to remind employees to be more attentive, but they resisted giving drivers extra time to verify labels. Hana then suspended the busiest sorting line for three days, despite warnings that major customers might leave. This move sent a shock wave through the cooperative, giving the staff time to compare records without a growing pile of parcels demanding immediate attention.

A school environmental team noticed floating litter collecting along a canal after a weekend festival. The students built a simple model to explore why material accumulated at one bend instead of moving evenly downstream. Their account concerns the model, not a forecast for the real canal.
Three conditions shaped the results. First, a small fan created air movement that pushed the floating pieces sideways toward the same bank. Second, a rough strip along the model's edge caught passing material. Third, a narrowed channel increased the pile near the bend. When the students made the channel extremely narrow, pieces arrived faster than the trap could be emptied. The team grouped these findings under air movement, bank surfaces, and channel design.
For one trial, the model began with 6 floating pieces in the collection area. Its feeding device made the total triple every two minutes. No pieces were removed during that trial, and the students assumed the same rate continued for four minutes. They later compared two clean-up methods: a wide net across the water and a small basket near the bank. The net caught more material but blocked the channel, while the basket left room for water to pass but needed frequent emptying.
After the trials, the students explained that a tool could solve one difficulty while creating another. They advised the organizers to consider the canal's shape and the time needed to remove collected material before choosing equipment. A larger device would not necessarily work better in every part of the canal.

explain: 風扇產生的 air movement（空氣流動）把漂浮物推向同一岸；粗糙邊緣負責攔住物件，作用不同。

At the annual Riverport Book Fair, publishers once occupied separate rows according to their home districts. The final afternoon ended with a formal sales report: each district's manager read out a total while other sellers remained beside their own tables. Visitors often left before this ceremony began. Intended to recognize local effort, the arrangement made a reading festival feel like a contest between neighbors.
During one especially tense year, a disagreement over parking fees spread into the exhibition hall. Sellers from two districts accused each other of receiving better spaces, and some refused to recommend books stocked by the other group. A storm then damaged the entrance roof, forcing several stalls to move. Arguments over the remaining dry areas threatened the fair's cooperative spirit. The committee considered closing early, although repairs allowed the fair to continue.
Mira, a volunteer who delivered lunches to the sellers, suggested a different closing activity. Instead of announcing district totals, each seller would introduce a favorite book from another stall. She believed that sharing readers mattered more than defending separate territories. The committee accepted her proposal on the final morning. During the introductions, sellers crossed the hall to exchange recommendations, and visitors stayed to listen.
Later fairs kept the activity, though the districts still received private sales reports. Mira received credit years later, after an organizer found her handwritten suggestion. The change did not remove every disagreement, but it rescued a fair that had been hanging by a thread. An outsider’s modest proposal had changed the event’s tone.
q: What motivated Mira to propose the new activity?
choices: She wanted private reports to become public information.
She hoped better sales would pay for the roof repairs.
She wanted districts to compete on book recommendations.
She valued closer ties among readers and booksellers.
explain: 她認為分享讀者比守住各區地盤重要，因此提議的目的在建立讀者與書商間的連結。並非公開私下報告、籌修繕費，或換另一種形式競賽。

subject: english
passage:
A city archive has enough money to restore only part of its collection each year. To attract donations, it often displays beautifully illustrated travel diaries in its publicity. The drawings are easy to appreciate, so the diaries bring in funds and attract first-time visitors. Some have become symbols of the city's past. Yet hundreds of plain account books remain in storage, even though they record the work of people rarely represented in the attractive diaries.
Choosing which documents deserve treatment is therefore more complicated than choosing the most popular display. Staff may be influenced by a donor's interests or by pressure to support an anniversary exhibition. They also consider whether an item can survive treatment and has a complete copy elsewhere. A record that looks unremarkable may contain the only surviving information about a vanished neighborhood.
One planning method estimates the work required to save each document and examines how quickly untreated damage is spreading. [X] Another method emphasizes the uniqueness of the information, even when restoring a document would be expensive. Neither method simply counts visitors to an exhibition, although public interest remains important for raising money.
Beautiful diaries deserve care, and their ability to attract donations should not be dismissed. However, allowing their appearance to determine the entire restoration program would leave other voices unheard. Publicity should also introduce less decorative records. An archive preserves a community most effectively when its choices reflect the variety of lives within it, rather than the visual appeal of a few famous objects.
q: Which factor can influence restoration decisions?
choices: Whether donors prefer particular kinds of material.
Whether having a full copy guarantees restoration.
Whether plain records repeat the diaries' content.
Whether unique diaries are safe from physical damage.
explain: 文中明說捐款者偏好可能影響修復選擇。有完整複本不保證入選；帳簿可能保存日記沒有的資訊；獨特性也不表示文件不會受損。

subject: english
passage:
In the hill town of Bellridge, an old textile mill has become a popular weekend market. It brought visitors and jobs to formerly empty streets. For nearby households, however, the revival has a cost: the streets they once used for shopping and deliveries are now difficult to enter.
On market days, private traffic is stopped at the district boundary. Residents must carry groceries from a distant car park or pay for the market operator's electric carts. The public bus still runs, but its stop was moved uphill to make room for visitor coaches. Older residents find the climb difficult. Shopkeepers also report that morning deliveries sometimes arrive after their stores open because the entrance gate is shared with market stalls.
Many residents blame the operator, which received permission to reserve the central street for stalls in exchange for maintaining it. They say the town values tourist spending above everyday access to public space. Some have covered their windows with protest signs, while several shops have stopped selling market tickets.
The operator answers that the road restrictions were imposed by the council to reduce accidents. It attributes delivery delays to the narrow streets and says the town's limited bus service existed long before the market. It has offered free cart rides for residents over seventy and proposed moving the bus stop closer to homes. Yet no timetable has been agreed upon. Residents say the age rule leaves many people without assistance, and they want guaranteed access rather than temporary favors. With each side disputing responsibility, a quick improvement seems unlikely.
q: Which heading best captures the passage?
choices: How a market solved a declining town's problems.
Why free transport settled a street access dispute.
The hidden costs of reviving a local town center.
A council plan to swap tourism for local shopping.
explain: 全文由市場復甦帶出居民交通困難及責任爭論，hidden costs 是「隱藏代價」，能涵蓋效益背後的生活負擔。

subject: english
passage:
A materials laboratory is examining why reusable shopping labels become unreadable. Its first test used tags printed on paper and covered with a thin film. During repeated washing, the film lifted at the edges, and water reached the ink. Darker printing made the words clearer for a short time, but it did not prevent water from entering. The team therefore began investigating three other parts of the design.
① Each tag includes a woven backing beneath the printed layer. The first research group is replacing this backing with a tighter weave, hoping to reduce the amount of water moving through it. ② The backing is classified as a textile, rather than a coating. Researchers measure how much moisture each sample retains after washing.
A second group is studying the edge seal. The laboratory compares three shapes, labeled arc, step, and wave. So far, the wave seal has admitted the least water during bending tests. ③ The next trial will compare the seals after thirty washes. The team expects ordinary movement to reveal weaknesses that a single wash might miss.
A third group studies support fibers inside the tag. They help the label regain its shape after folding. Broken fibers may leave gaps through which moisture enters. This group has examined damaged tags but has not yet tested a replacement fiber in a washing machine.
④ Improving the structure deserves more research funding than changing the ink. ⑤ A successful tag should balance easy reuse with an attractive appearance. The laboratory has not announced a final design, and the next stage will test whether the promising changes work together.
q: Which outline best represents the main research directions?
choices: Ink failure → trials of three new printing methods.
Limited ink benefits → backing, seals, support fibers.
Three successful materials → a final commercial label.
Washing damage → comparisons of shopper behavior.
explain: 文章先說加深墨色僅暫時改善清晰度，再分為底襯、邊緣封合與支撐纖維三條研究方向。並非三種新印刷法，也尚未完成商品設計或研究購物行為。

The first research group is replacing this backing with a tighter weave, hoping to reduce the amount of water moving through it. ② The backing is classified as a textile, rather than a coating. Researchers measure how much moisture each sample retains after washing.

So far, the wave seal has admitted the least water during bending tests. ③ The next trial will compare the seals after thirty washes. The history of the Cedar District's equipment exchange began with a locked cupboard, not a public building. During a street meeting, several families proposed storing equipment together. Each household contributed a small amount, and a shopkeeper offered space behind his counter. Members wrote their names in a notebook whenever they borrowed something.
As membership grew, the notebook became difficult to manage. Two people sometimes arrived expecting the same item, while others returned equipment without telling the shopkeeper. The organizers introduced numbered cards and separate return times. They did not charge an extra borrowing fee, although members had to pay for damage they caused. Later, a housing project brought many new residents into the district. Requests for equipment increased so rapidly that the original cupboard could no longer serve the neighborhood.
Two volunteers responded independently. Mara opened a second collection in an unused classroom, using money raised at a weekend sale. Across the district, Dev obtained permission to store another collection inside an apartment building. Both asked experienced residents to teach short repair lessons before lending unfamiliar equipment. Neither volunteer manufactured tools; their contribution was to organize access and reduce avoidable damage.
Eventually, the separate collections adopted one booking system. Members could see where an item was available and reserve it before traveling. The exchange continued to change: some residents requested garden equipment, while others wanted devices for recording music. What had begun as a cupboard became a network shaped by changing neighborhood needs.
q: Which title best captures the whole account?
choices: The career of a local equipment manufacturer
The growth of a local equipment exchange
The advantages of buying equipment together
The design of safer household power tools

In a classroom design project, students investigated why a prominent symbol did not always make an instruction easier to follow. The class suspected that decoration might attract attention while competing with the information people actually needed. To examine this possibility, they constructed a model station with four possible exits.
Volunteers were assigned to one of three sign conditions. The first used plain arrows, the second added a colorful photograph, and the third combined the photograph with a moving border on a screen. Every sign displayed the same destination name and pointed in the correct direction. Each volunteer saw only one condition, and all began at the same distance from the model. The students recorded both the time taken to notice the sign and the time needed to select an exit. They also counted incorrect choices.
The decorated signs were noticed sooner. However, after noticing them, volunteers in both decorated conditions took longer to choose an exit than those seeing plain arrows. Incorrect choices were also more frequent with decoration, especially when the border moved. The students concluded that attracting the eye and communicating directions were separate achievements. The photograph and movement drew attention, but they also made the useful arrow harder to pick out.
The teacher cautioned that a model station could not represent every busy public space. Even so, the results suggested why an especially eye-catching sign might fail during a hurried journey. The class recommended testing a sign's effect on decisions rather than judging it merely by how quickly people looked at it.
q: Which sequence describes how the report develops?
choices: A dispute, a personal story, then an apology
A definition, a historical survey, then a prediction
A question, a test, then findings and implications
A discovery, opposing opinions, then a compromise
explain: 先提出裝飾是否妨礙指示的問題，再說實驗方法、結果與應用限制；implications 是結果的意涵。

At a small community theater, a painted landscape can change shape before the audience's eyes. The scenery team uses folding panels, light boards joined with cloth strips. Aya, the workshop leader, prefers these strips to metal hinges because they allow the panels to fold quietly during a performance. A squeak at the wrong moment could interrupt a whispered line. The boards are painted on both sides so that turning them reveals a new location without requiring a second set.
To create a narrow street, stagehands arrange three panels at sharp angles. For an open courtyard, they spread the same boards into a broad curve. A forest scene requires two boards in front and one behind, leaving a gap through which actors can appear. The exact angle must be tested from several seats: a scene that looks convincing from the center may expose an actor waiting at the side. These arrangements let a small group present several places with very little storage space.
In the theater's early years, experienced stagehands recorded successful arrangements in sketchbooks. They explained why a particular gap was necessary and taught newcomers how to protect painted surfaces while folding them. The drawings became a practical memory of earlier performances, allowing techniques to pass from one group to the next.
During a show, the scenery team follows cues from a stage manager. Yet the process is fluid. If an actor needs extra time to finish a speech, the manager may hold a cue; if an entrance is missed, a panel may be moved later than planned. A skilled stagehand therefore learns the play's rhythm as carefully as the position of every board.
q: Why does Aya favor cloth strips for joining panels?
choices: They make both panel faces easier to paint.
They keep panels open without stagehands.
They allow quieter changes between scenes.
They give heavy actors stronger support.

When Nora Vale began helping at a town records office, she expected to spend her days copying dates. Instead, a bundle of damaged letters changed her career. The letters described a market square that official maps showed as empty. Vale visited older residents, compared their accounts, and discovered that the maps had recorded property boundaries while leaving daily activities unmarked.
Vale later organized a public collection of neighborhood memories. Rather than filing every account under a single street name, she linked each one to the speaker's occupation, age, and reason for remembering it. This approach helped visitors understand why witnesses sometimes described the same corner differently. Vale also insisted that uncertain dates be marked openly instead of being silently corrected.
Her wider influence came through teaching. The first volunteers trained by Vale established memory projects in other towns and passed her methods to their own teams. Although her original collection occupied only a small room, the habits of careful listening and explicit uncertainty spread far beyond its shelves.
Vale compared historical accounts to windows facing different directions. No single window offered the whole view, but each revealed something the others could not. She did not argue that every memory was equally accurate; contradictions still required investigation. Her point was that disagreement could guide a better question rather than justify immediate rejection. Some officials found the method inconvenient because it resisted a tidy, uniform story. To me, her willingness to preserve that complexity was an admirable contribution to public understanding.

choices: The unexpected value of a damaged market map
Why towns should replace maps with interviews
Nora Vale and a lasting approach to local memory
How records offices can reduce their filing costs
